lead: A window shows a small part of a large drawing. A line may start and end outside the window yet cross the visible area. Clipping keeps the part inside and throws the rest away, so the rasteriser plots only visible pixels and coordinates stay small. Cohen–Sutherland labels each end point with a 4-bit region code and cuts one boundary at a time. Liang–Barsky writes the line as P(u) and solves four inequalities for the visible range of u.
prereq: You need: the window rectangle and its mapping to the screen from 2.5, and line drawing with DDA or Bresenham from Unit 1, Output primitives.

blocks.text: The window is the rectangle xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax, ymin ≤ y ≤ ymax. Clipping a segment P1P2 returns only the part inside that rectangle. Three outcomes exist: fully inside, so it passes unchanged; fully outside, so nothing is drawn; or crossing a boundary, so it becomes a shorter segment. At least one new end point sits on a boundary; the other may be an original point already inside.

Clipping saves work. A line from (−4000, 20) to (5000, 30) covers about 9000 pixel steps, but only a few hundred are on screen; clipping first shortens it to those steps. It also keeps coordinates small for 16-bit integer rasterisers.
One rule keeps both algorithms correct: a new end point is always found along the original line. Pushing x onto xmin while leaving y unchanged slides the end point off the line and changes the slope.

Give each end point a 4-bit code. Bit 3, value 8: y > ymax (above). Bit 2, value 4: y < ymin (below). Bit 1, value 2: x > xmax (right). Bit 0, value 1: x < xmin (left). Inside or on the boundary: 0000.

items: If both codes are 0000, accept the whole segment and stop.
If code(P1) AND code(P2) is not zero, both ends lie beyond the same boundary, so reject and stop.
Otherwise pick an end point with a nonzero code and one of its set bits, and clip against that boundary.
Replace that end point by the intersection and go back to step 1. Each pass clears one bit, so the loop ends after at most four intersections.

blocks.text: For the vertical boundary x = c:  y = y1 + (c − x1)(y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1)
blocks.where: (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) are the current end points in world coordinates, and c is xmin or xmax.

blocks.text: For the horizontal boundary y = c:  x = x1 + (c − y1)(x2 − x1)/(y2 − y1)
blocks.where: c is ymin or ymax; all other symbols are as above.

blocks.text: Write the segment as P(u) = P1 + u(P2 − P1) with 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, where dx = x2 − x1 and dy = y2 − y1. A point is inside when xmin ≤ x1 + u·dx ≤ xmax and ymin ≤ y1 + u·dy ≤ ymax. Each inequality rearranges into p·u ≤ q.
Start with u1 = 0 and u2 = 1, then walk the four rows.

items: p = 0: the line is parallel to that boundary. If q < 0 the whole line is outside, so reject. If q ≥ 0 this boundary cannot cut the line, so ignore it.
p < 0: the line enters the window across this boundary. r = q/p is a lower bound, so u1 = max(u1, r).
p > 0: the line leaves here. r = q/p is an upper bound, so u2 = min(u2, r).
After the four rows, if u1 > u2 the line misses the window; otherwise draw from P(u1) to P(u2).

blocks.text: For the worked example p = (−12, 12, −6, 6) and q = (−4, 10, −1, 5), so r = 1/3, 5/6, 1/6, 5/6, giving u1 = 1/3 and u2 = 5/6. The x = 8 and y = 6 tests both land on (8, 6).
Liang–Barsky needs no loop and at most four tests. Nicholl–Lee–Nicholl sorts the window and corners into regions to make fewer comparisons; only the name is expected.

figure.caption: The loop computes codes, accepts or rejects at once, and otherwise cuts one boundary at a time. After one intersection the codes are recomputed; this turns (−2, 1) into (2, 3) and then (10, 7) into (8, 6).

spec.title: Cohen–Sutherland decision loop
spec.aria: A flowchart that computes end-point codes, accepts or rejects the line, and otherwise intersects with a boundary and loops back with the new endpoint.

examples.question: Clip the line from P1(−2, 1) to P2(10, 7) against the window xmin = 2, xmax = 8, ymin = 2, ymax = 6. Use (a) Cohen–Sutherland and (b) Liang–Barsky, and state the visible end points.
steps: Code of P1(−2, 1): left bit 1 and below bit 4, so 0101. Code of P2(10, 7): right bit 2 and above bit 8, so 1010.
AND is 0000, so not rejected; neither code is 0000, so not accepted.
Cut P2 at y = 6: x = 2 + (6 − 3)(10 − 2)/(7 − 3) = 8. New P2 = (8, 6), code 0000 because the boundary counts as inside.
examples.answer: The visible part of the line runs from (2, 3) to (8, 6); Cohen–Sutherland and Liang–Barsky give the same answer.

traps: Clamping one coordinate onto the boundary and leaving the other unchanged slides the end point off the line and changes the slope; compute the intersection along the line.
Reading a zero AND as acceptance. AND = 0 only means rejection is impossible; clip unless both codes are 0000.
Swapping the Liang–Barsky updates. p < 0 tightens u1 with max, p > 0 tightens u2 with min; swapped, an invisible line gets drawn.
Treating a boundary point as outside. With ≤ and ≥ it is inside and gets code 0000; strict inequalities can make a corner-touching line loop forever.

quiz.q: List the four Cohen–Sutherland region bits with their values, and give the code of a point inside the window.
quiz.a: Above y > ymax: 8. Below y < ymin: 4. Right x > xmax: 2. Left x < xmin: 1. Inside: 0000.

quiz.q: Why does a nonzero bitwise AND of the two end-point codes prove the whole segment is outside?
quiz.a: The same bit set in both means both end points lie beyond the same boundary of the convex window. A straight segment between two points on the same outer side cannot re-enter, so every point of it is outside.

quiz.q: Clip (0, 0) to (10, 5) against x from 2 to 8 and y from 1 to 4 using Liang–Barsky.
Give the Cohen–Sutherland codes of A(9, 5), B(1, 0) and C(5, 3) for the window x from 2 to 8, y from 1 to 4.
quiz.a: A: x > 8 gives 2, y > 4 gives 8, code 1010. B: x < 2 gives 1, y < 1 gives 4, code 0101. C: inside, code 0000.

quiz.q: Two end points have codes 0001 and 0010. Can the line be rejected at once? What happens next?
quiz.a: AND = 0000, so no rejection; the codes differ, so it is not accepted either. Code 0001 marks an end left of the window and code 0010 marks an end right of it, so one end is cut against x = xmin and the other against x = xmax. Recompute the codes. If the two new y-values still put both ends beyond the same horizontal boundary, reject; otherwise clip again against y = ymin or y = ymax.

quiz.q: In Liang–Barsky, what does p = 0 with q < 0 mean, and why is the line rejected?
quiz.a: p = 0 means the line is parallel to that boundary, so u cannot change the side it is on. q < 0 puts the whole line on the outer side of that boundary, for example dy = 0 with y1 < ymin, so no value of u can be inside.

quiz.q: State the two Cohen–Sutherland intersection formulas, for x = c and y = c.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every GPU has scissor rectangles and clip volumes in hardware, so tests like these run on billions of vertices per second. Cyrus–Beck generalises the same parametric idea to any convex clip region; clipping against the six planes of a three-dimensional view volume is one use. The same boundary-by-boundary idea becomes Sutherland–Hodgman for polygons, and a photo editor's clipping mask applies it to pixels. Useful search terms: Liang–Barsky derivation, Cyrus–Beck clipping, guard-band clipping, scissor test.
